rv.q: Promising but unpolished sci-fi drama explores Big Tech, Jewish identity and the responsibility never to forget the past
Memoriam is a moving play that focuses on the social responsibility of ensuring stories do not die with us.
That said, there are some substantial moral and ethical questions raised in this intriguing and engaging production.
While the production delivers on much of its potential, there remains room for greater finesse in its execution to give this thought-provoking story the impact its premise promises.
There is some genuinely good work here both in the script and from the players.

More broadly, there is a sense of artificiality both to the script and to Daniel Goldman’s direction, as though the cast are reading off a list of bullet points, answering all the misgivings someone might have about preserving a Holocaust survivor’s memories.
Memoriam is a story that is so relevant, so poignant, and so beautifully told that I would defy anyone not to be moved by what has been created.
Ellie Wintour’s sleek minimal set and costumes with Jonathan Chan’s spectacular lighting combine to make the Southwark Borough Large glint like a spaceship...
Surprisingly, maybe even shockingly, there are moments of humour against the horror; a levity to balance the depth of awfulness.
Memoriam makes a compelling family drama of the genuine conundrum of how to keep history alive when the last witnesses to it are dead.
Memoriam is the definition of challenging and thought provoking theatre.
Nevertheless, the production remains accessible and compelling throughout.
Memoriam is a thought-provoking and moving piece of theatre, and will have you thinking about your memories and the memories of those you love.

And all of a sudden what could have been a fascinating analysis of a new (albeit fictional) medium for telling the ghastly history of the Holocaust, gets lost in a mini-parable on the evils of capitalism.
There's something really special hiding within Memoriam . It just needs a little more editing itself.
The central concept is undoubtedly strong, offering plenty of food for thought, but the script doesn't always do it justice.
Her somewhat bleak but frequently humorous one-act play… intriguing and thought provoking

The play's serious intent is not in question, but the trouble is the production has been staged in the round and director Daniel Goldman has failed to get his cast to act in the round so that the entire audience hears what is being said.
I think this play is not fully realising its potential and, to be honest, not quite trusting itself in seeing the truly bigger story that is trying to be heard.

Thought-provoking theatre such as this remains sadly the exception to a general rule, particularly in the West End, so, if you want to be both educated and entertained, consider spending some time watching this family decide whether it is right to walk down memory lane.
Memoriam is a thought-provoking exploration of memory, ownership and responsibility.
The family scenes and moral debates about commercialising the memories are where the play really flies.
Daniel Goldman’s direction skilfully weaves the polemic into a warm-hearted family saga, but ultimately both are a little compromised.
There is food for thought in this finely performed, but somewhat haphazard tale.

cn.t: A thought-provoking sci-fi premise about commodifying Holocaust memories generates compelling ethical questions, but the execution feels uneven. Beverley Klein's performance as the survivor shines, though the play struggles to fully realize its ambitious concept.
